searchDocs.title: Chrome, Edge, Brave and other Chromium browsers​
searchDocs.content: 1 Download texttoscratch-extension.zip and unzip it.  2 Open chrome://extensions and switch on Developer mode (top right).  3 Click Load unpacked and choose the unzipped folder (the one containing manifest.json).  4 Open any project in the Scratch editor. Text Code appears in the purple menu bar.

searchDocs.title: Firefox​
searchDocs.content: Unzip the same download, open about:debugging#/runtime/this-firefox, click Load Temporary Add-on…, and pick its manifest.json. Firefox removes temporary add-ons when it restarts.

searchDocs.title: No install? Use the web editor​
searchDocs.content: The web editor is the same editor as a plain web page. Click Open .sb3, code, then Download .sb3 and load the file into Scratch with File → Load from your computer.  Where is my code saved? Your source files are stored inside the Scratch project (in a collapsed Stage comment). Saving the project in Scratch saves your code too, and opening it again brings the code back.

searchDocs.title: Create a project​
searchDocs.content: tts init my-game   my-game/ project.sb3 optional: a project saved from Scratch, used for its art and sounds tsconfig.json gives VS Code the same types and errors src/ Stage.ts the stage Player.ts one file per sprite (file name = sprite name) Player/ images here become Player's costumes (png, svg, jpg) idle.png walk1.png Stage/ images here become backdrops

searchDocs.title: Build​
searchDocs.content: tts build my-game   This writes dist/my-game.sb3; open it in Scratch with File → Load from your computer. tts watch my-game rebuilds on every save.  Each build also writes .tts/scratch.d.ts and .tts/sprites.d.ts, so VS Code autocompletes your sprite, costume and sound names.

searchDocs.title: Image folders​
searchDocs.content: Every image in src/<Sprite>/ becomes a costume named after its file (run1.png becomes the costume run1). Costumes are added in name order; an image with the same name as an existing costume replaces it. SVG, PNG and JPG are supported.

searchDocs.title: Round trip with Scratch​
searchDocs.content: Build, open the .sb3 in Scratch, and draw or edit art there.File → Save to your computer as my-game/project.sb3.Build again: your art comes from project.sb3 and your logic from src/.

searchDocs.title: Differences from JavaScript
searchDocs.content: Differences from JavaScript Your code runs as Scratch blocks, so it follows Scratch's rules. Here's what to keep in mind. Topic	What happensbreak, continue, switch	Not supported. Use a flag in the loop condition, or return from a function. Variable values	Kept between runs (green flag clicks). Reset them in whenFlag. Variables inside functions	Become sprite variables, so they aren't safe across recursion. Value-returning calls	At most one per statement. Split f(a) + f(b) into two variables. Loop conditions	Can't call value-returning functions or use ?:. Compute the value into a variable first. == / ===	Scratch equality: compares numbers numerically, text case-insensitively ("A" === "a" is true). %	Result takes the sign of the divisor (-1 % 3 is 2). sin, cos, ...	Use degrees. Functions	Belong to their sprite. To run code elsewhere, use broadcast. Objects	Only for state ({ score: 0 }). No classes, no objects at runtime. Lists	Hold numbers and text. No nested arrays. Timing	Like Scratch, loops yield once per frame unless the function is marked /** @warp */.

searchDocs.title: Files are sprites​
searchDocs.content: File	BecomesStage.ts	the Stage Player.ts	the sprite named Player (it's created if it doesn't exist yet)  Code at the top level of a file can only declare things: variables, functions, and event handlers.

searchDocs.title: Variables​
searchDocs.content: let speed = 5; // "for this sprite only" variable export const game = { score: 0 }; // global variables: score const GRAVITY = 0.8; // constant, inlined (no variable) const items: string[] = []; // list   Code	Scratchlet x = 0 at the top of a sprite file	variable for this sprite only (every clone gets its own copy) export const state = { a: 0, b: "" }	global variables a and b, used as state.a from any file export let x = 0	global variable (only the file that declares it can assign it) const N = 5	inlined literal const list: number[] = [1, 2]	list with starting items let i = 0 inside a function or event	a sprite variable with a unique name  Initial values must be literals. They're saved in the project as the variable's starting value.

searchDocs.title: Using shared state​
searchDocs.content: TypeScript doesn't let other files assign to an imported let, so share state through an object:  Stage.ts export const game = { score: 0, lives: 3 };   Enemy.ts import { game } from "./Stage"; onMessage("hit", () => { game.lives--; });

searchDocs.title: Events​
searchDocs.content: Event handlers must be at the top level:  whenFlag(() => { ... }); whenKey("space", () => { ... }); whenClicked(() => { ... }); whenBackdrop("level2", () => { ... }); whenGreater("timer", 10, () => { ... }); onMessage("game over", () => { ... }); onClone(() => { ... });

searchDocs.title: Control flow​
searchDocs.content: Code	Blockif (c) { } else { }	if / else while (c) { }	repeat until not c while (true) { } / forever(() => { })	forever for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) { }	set + repeat until repeat(10, () => { })	repeat 10 waitUntil(() => cond)	wait until cond ? a : b	if / else into a temporary variable return	stop this script

searchDocs.title: Functions = custom blocks​
searchDocs.content: /** @warp */ function drawSquare(size: number, filled: boolean) { ... }   Parameters can be number, string or boolean (boolean parameters become hexagonal inputs)./** @warp */ turns on Run without screen refresh.Functions can return a value; it's passed back through a hidden __ret variable.Functions belong to their sprite. To run code in another sprite, broadcast a message.

searchDocs.title: Sprite properties: me​
searchDocs.content: me.x += 5; // change x by 5 me.y = 0; // set y to 0 me.direction = 90; // point in direction 90 me.size = 150; // set size to 150 % me.visible = false; // hide me.rotationStyle = "left-right"; me.draggable = true; if (me.costumeName === "jump") { ... }

searchDocs.content: Code	Blocka + b (numbers)	+ a + b, `Score: ${s}` (strings)	join - * / %	arithmetic < > <= >= === !==	comparisons && || !	and / or / not Math.floor(x), Math.abs(x), Math.sqrt(x), ...	floor of, ... Math.round(x), Math.min(a, b), Math.max(a, b), Math.random()	round / computed / pick random random(1, 10)	pick random 1 to 10 str.length, str[i], str.includes(s)	length / letter of / contains list[i], list.length, list.includes(x), list.indexOf(x)	list reporters

searchDocs.title: Typed asset names​
searchDocs.content: Sprite, costume, backdrop and sound names are checked against your project:  switchCostume("jmup"); // ~~~~~~ Argument of type '"jmup"' is not assignable to parameter of type 'CostumeName'.

searchDocs.title: 1. Make the sprites in Scratch​
searchDocs.content: Create these sprites in the Scratch editor. Draw them however you like; only the names matter, because the code uses them.  Sprite	Costumes	What it isPlayer	idle, walk1, walk2, jump, physics	the character; physics is a plain solid rectangle used for collisions Level	level1	every platform and floor, drawn on one costume Coin	coin	a collectible Goal	flag	touch it to win Stage	sky, win	backdrops    Use image files instead With the CLI, you can drop image files into src/Player/, src/Level/ and so on. Each image becomes a costume named after its file. In the editor, you can drag images onto a sprite tile.

searchDocs.title: 2. Open the text editor​
searchDocs.content: Click Text Code in the menu bar. The code editor covers the blocks area; your stage and sprite list stay where they were.    The Sprites pane on the left lists every sprite. Faded tiles have no code yet, and their hand-made blocks are left alone.Click a tile to create or open that sprite's file. Each sprite gets one file, and Stage.ts is the stage.Build compiles; Build & Run (Ctrl+S) compiles, loads the project and clicks the green flag.

searchDocs.title: 3. Shared game state — Stage.ts​
searchDocs.content: Click the Stage tile and write:  Stage.ts // Global state shared by every sprite. export const game = { coins: 0, won: false }; whenFlag(() => { switchBackdrop("sky"); game.coins = 0; game.won = false; showVariable(game.coins); }); onMessage("win", () => { game.won = true; switchBackdrop("win"); });   export const game = { ... } creates the global Scratch variables coins and won. Other files import { game } from "./Stage"and can read or change them, for example game.coins++.  Variables keep their values Like Scratch, variables are not reset when you press the green flag. That's why whenFlag sets game.coins = 0.

searchDocs.title: 4. The level — Level.ts​
searchDocs.content: The level is just a sprite whose costume is all the ground. The player collides with anything drawn on it.  Level.ts whenFlag(() => { goTo(0, 0); goToBack(); });

searchDocs.title: 5. The player — Player.ts​
searchDocs.content: This is the heart of the game. Start with the tuning values and the player's state:  Player.ts import { game } from "./Stage"; // Tuning const GRAVITY = 0.8; const JUMP = 12; const ACCEL = 1.2; const FRICTION = 0.8; const STEP_UP = 6; // how many pixels of slope/step we climb automatically const SPAWN_X = -200; const SPAWN_Y = -100; let vx = 0; let vy = 0; let onGround = false;   const values with a literal are inlined (no variable is created). let variables at the top of a sprite file become "for this sprite only" variables.

searchDocs.title: Collisions​
searchDocs.content: Each axis moves separately. If a move puts us inside the level, we step back out pixel by pixel:  /** @warp */ function moveX(dx: number) { me.x += dx; if (touching("Level")) { let lift = 0; while (touching("Level") && lift < STEP_UP) { me.y += 1; lift++; } if (touching("Level")) { me.y -= lift; const back = dx > 0 ? -1 : 1; while (touching("Level")) me.x += back; vx = 0; } } } /** @warp */ function moveY(dy: number) { me.y += dy; onGround = false; if (touching("Level")) { const back = dy > 0 ? -1 : 1; while (touching("Level")) me.y += back; if (dy < 0) onGround = true; vy = 0; } }   Functions become custom blocks. /** @warp */ ticks Run without screen refresh, so the collision loops finish in a single frame.

searchDocs.title: Animation​
searchDocs.content: function animate() { if (vx > 0.5) pointInDirection(90); if (vx < -0.5) pointInDirection(-90); if (!onGround) { switchCostume("jump"); } else if (Math.abs(vx) > 1) { switchCostume(Math.floor(timer() * 8) % 2 === 0 ? "walk1" : "walk2"); } else { switchCostume("idle"); } } function respawn() { goTo(SPAWN_X, SPAWN_Y); vx = 0; vy = 0; }   The editor knows your costume names, so it autocompletes them:

searchDocs.title: The game loop​
searchDocs.content: whenFlag(() => { me.rotationStyle = "left-right"; goToFront(); respawn(); while (!game.won) { if (keyPressed("right arrow") || keyPressed("d")) vx += ACCEL; if (keyPressed("left arrow") || keyPressed("a")) vx -= ACCEL; vx *= FRICTION; vy -= GRAVITY; if (onGround && (keyPressed("up arrow") || keyPressed("w") || keyPressed("space"))) vy = JUMP; // Collide using a fixed box so animation frames can't push us into walls. // (Costume changes aren't drawn until the loop finishes, so it never shows.) switchCostume("physics"); moveX(vx); moveY(vy); animate(); if (me.y < -170) respawn(); } sayFor(`I got ${game.coins} coins!`, 3); });   Why the physics costume? Walking and jumping costumes have different shapes. If the legs poke out further in one frame, switching costume can push the player into the floor. Doing all the collision checks with one plain rectangle avoids that. The switch happens within a single frame, so the rectangle is never drawn.

searchDocs.title: 6. Coins with clones — Coin.ts​
searchDocs.content: Coin.ts import { game } from "./Stage"; // Coin positions (lists). const coinX = [-70, 55, 140, -10, 190]; const coinY = [-35, 25, -115, -80, 100]; // The original coin is invisible and stamps out clones at each position. whenFlag(() => { me.visible = false; for (let i = 0; i < coinX.length; i++) { goTo(coinX[i], coinY[i]); createClone(); } }); onClone(() => { me.visible = true; waitUntil(() => touching("Player")); game.coins++; repeat(5, () => { me.y += 4; changeEffect("ghost", 20); }); deleteClone(); });   Arrays become Scratch lists. Indexes start at 0 in your code; the compiler adds 1 for Scratch.

searchDocs.title: 7. The goal — Goal.ts​
searchDocs.content: Goal.ts whenFlag(() => { goTo(200, 82); waitUntil(() => touching("Player")); broadcast("win"); });

searchDocs.title: 8. Build & Run​
searchDocs.content: Press Build & Run (or Ctrl+S). Use the arrow keys or WASD to run and jump. Grab the coins and reach the flag.

searchDocs.title: Mistakes are caught before you run​
searchDocs.content: Misspell a costume and the editor underlines it straight away. Press Build and the problem is listed with its file and line. Click it to jump there.

searchDocs.title: What your code became​
searchDocs.content: Close the editor (✕) to see the blocks TextToScratch generated. They're ordinary Scratch blocks, so you can read them, learn from them, or keep editing by hand.    Code owns its sprites When a sprite has a code file, Build replaces that sprite's blocks with the compiled ones. Sprites without a code file keep their hand-made blocks, so you can mix both styles in one project.

searchDocs.title: Next steps​
searchDocs.content: Read the language guide to see how TypeScript maps onto Scratch.Browse the API reference for every available block.Check how it differs from JavaScript before you write bigger projects.

searchDocs.title: Why text?​
searchDocs.content: Types catch mistakes. The real TypeScript compiler checks everything, including the names of your sprites, costumes, backdrops and sounds. A typo is an error before the game ever runs.Bigger projects stay readable. Functions, constants, comments, and search and replace all work, and there are no 300-block scripts to scroll through.It's still Scratch. The output uses only standard blocks, so anyone can open it in Scratch and see exactly what your code became.

searchDocs.title: Three ways to use it​
searchDocs.content: Best forBrowser extension	Coding inside the Scratch editor next to your stage and sprites. Recommended. Web editor	Trying it out with no install: open an .sb3, edit, download. CLI	VS Code, git, and keeping your art as image files in folders.

searchDocs.title: A taste​
searchDocs.content: Player.ts import { game } from "./Stage"; whenFlag(() => { goTo(0, 0); forever(() => { if (keyPressed("right arrow")) me.x += 5; if (keyPressed("left arrow")) me.x -= 5; if (touching("Coin")) game.score++; }); });   Each file is one sprite (Stage.ts is the stage). whenFlag, forever, keyPressed and touching are Scratch blocks.me is the current sprite, and game is shared state that every sprite can read and change.  Ready? Install the extension, then follow the platformer tutorial.
